title: How Dissociative Identity Disorder Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain dissociative identity disorder (DID), formerly called multiple personality disorder. They cover the core concept of a host personality with alters that emerge under stress, often tied to childhood trauma, and how the disorder is distinct from split personality. They trace its history from the late eighteenth century through Eberhard Gmelin's early description, Louis Vivet, Pierre Janet, and Morton Prince, then the 1950s book The Three Faces of Eve, the 1973 book and film Sybil, and the 1970s-80s surge in diagnoses that Dr. Herbert Spiegel challenged. They describe the 1990s lawsuits against therapists, the renaming to DID, and the four related dissociative disorders (identity, amnesia, fugue, depersonalization). They discuss Herschel Walker's public disclosure and the hosts' debate over whether DID is real. The episode ends with listener mail from Tony, a recent returnee from Korea and engineering graduate, seeking career advice.

segments.title: Opening banter and alters
segments.summary: Hosts joke about alters and mention an online forum for people with DID. They introduce the name change from multiple personality disorder and the controversy around the diagnosis.

segments.title: What DID is and how it presents
segments.summary: Explanation of the host personality and alters, which can emerge under stress, often linked to early trauma as a coping mechanism. Alters may be aware of each other, may number from two to over a hundred, and can switch quickly. Symptoms include memory gaps, hallucinations, substance abuse, eating disorders, depression, anxiety and mood swings.

segments.title: Four related dissociative disorders
segments.summary: The old multiple personality disorder category was split into four dissociative disorders: identity disorder, amnesia, fugue, and depersonalization disorder. All share a protective function against trauma.

segments.title: Early history: Gmelin, Vivet, Janet and Prince
segments.summary: Late eighteenth-century understanding of the condition, then Eberhard Gmelin's late-1700s description of a patient with an alter. Louis Vivet is described as having six personalities, and Pierre Janet linked them to trauma. In 1905 Morton Prince claimed to cure a patient with hypnosis.

segments.title: The Three Faces of Eve
segments.summary: The 1957 book The Three Faces of Eve, by two psychiatrists about patient Eve White (real name Chris Costner Sizemore), popularized multiple personality disorder. Sizemore later wrote I'm Eve and said she was not cured and that the doctor used sodium pentothal and suggestion.

segments.title: Sybil and the 1970s MPD boom
segments.summary: The book Sybil, about patient Shirley Mason (pseudonym Sybil) treated by Cornelia Wilbur, and its film with Sally Field made MPD a sensation. Reported cases rose from about two hundred to eight thousand. Dr. Herbert Spiegel questioned the case, noting suggestibility and drug dependence, and the hosts discuss the later satanic ritual abuse panic and insanity-type legal defenses.

segments.title: Renaming to DID and lawsuits against therapists
segments.summary: Psychiatry renamed the condition dissociative identity disorder and returned to viewing alters as variations of the host personality. Patients sued therapists in the 1990s over hypnosis and drug-induced recall, and the hosts say the episode was a dark chapter for psychiatry.

segments.title: Is DID real? Herschel Walker and debate
segments.summary: Hosts discuss whether DID is real, agreeing the experience is real to sufferers but questioning the idea of separate personalities. They describe Herschel Walker's disclosure of DID and his reported memory gaps, including no memory of winning the Heisman Trophy.

segments.title: Listener mail: career advice for Tony
segments.summary: Tony, an engineering graduate who taught English in Korea, asks for career advice. Hosts suggest narrowing his job search, reflecting on what he loves, and not feeling bound by his degree.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and contact information and sign off.
